section_title: Why was some manna kept for later generations?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 31 Now the house of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. 32 Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” 33 So Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.” 34 And Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
35 The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan. 36 (Now an omer is a tenth of an ephah.)

context_lines: The bread receives its name and a description: white, resembling coriander seed, with a taste like honey wafers. God then commands that an omer be kept so later generations can see the food He gave Israel in the wilderness. The daily gift is also to become a lasting reminder.

Aaron places the jar before the Testimony, as commanded. The account looks ahead to the preserved memorial and sums up the long period of provision: Israel eats manna for forty years, until reaching the border of Canaan. God’s care extends through the journey, rather than ending with the first morning’s meal.

[Joshua 5:10–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/joshua/5.htm) later records the change after they enter the land. They eat its produce, and the manna ceases. The food has served the purpose God gave it while bringing His people to the place He promised.
common_interpretation_lines: The jar is read as a memorial of God’s faithful provision, meant to preserve the story for those who did not gather the food themselves. [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/16.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) both understand its preservation as part of the extraordinary provision God wanted later generations to remember.
god_plan_lines: [Hebrews 9:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/9.htm) explicitly recalls the gold jar of manna among the contents associated with the ark. The remembered wilderness provision becomes part of its description of Israel’s worship and sanctuary.

The manna image also appears in Jesus’ message to the church in [Revelation 2:12–17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/2.htm). A congregation facing pressure and teaching that encourages idol food is called to repent and remain faithful; Jesus promises hidden manna to the one who overcomes. The picture of food God gives is carried forward into His assurance to a struggling church. Revelation does not say that the historical jar itself will be opened and handed out.
